opus-5.5.text:
I think the real question is what the synthetic data is actually adding relative to the distribution you already have. When people say synthetic data "helps" or "hurts," what they're usually observing is whether it expands the support of the distribution in useful ways or just sharpens what's already there.

If you're generating data from a model trained on some underlying distribution, that data tends to concentrate around the modes. You get the high-probability, typical examples, and you lose the tails. For some tasks that's fine, even beneficial, because you're reinforcing patterns the model only partly learned. But if what matters for downstream performance lives in the long tail, like rare reasoning patterns, unusual languages, or edge cases in code, then repeatedly training on synthetic data can narrow the distribution. That's the intuition behind what people call model collapse: each round loses a bit of the diversity in the original data.

Where synthetic data really shines is when you have a verifier or some external signal of correctness. Math and code are the classic examples. You can generate lots of candidate solutions, check which ones are correct, and keep those. You're not just sampling from the model's distribution, you're filtering it toward a target distribution the model wasn't already hitting reliably. That's a genuinely new signal, so it helps.

It also depends on the mix. Synthetic data on its own rarely does well, but grounded in a substantial amount of real data, so the model stays anchored to the true distribution, it can fill gaps very effectively. So I'd look at three things: does it cover regions the real data underrepresents, is there a quality or correctness filter, and are you preserving enough real data to keep diversity? If those hold, synthetic data is a powerful tool. If not, you're mostly feeding the model its own reflection.

r001.rationale: The response says synthetic data alone rarely does well and explains that repeated synthetic training can lose tail diversity and narrow the distribution.

r002.rationale: It recommends grounding synthetic data in substantial real data to stay anchored to the true distribution and preserve diversity.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's really the crux of it. When I think about synthetic data, the first question I ask is: what's the gap between the distribution the model was trained on and the distribution where you actually want it to perform well? Synthetic data helps most when it fills a hole that the natural data just doesn't cover. If you're trying to get a model to reason through multi-step math problems, or follow very specific instruction formats, the web doesn't naturally contain a lot of that, so generating it can genuinely move the needle.

Where it hurts is when the synthetic data is drawn from essentially the same distribution the model already represents. If you're sampling from a model and feeding those samples back in, you're not adding new information, you're just reinforcing the modes the model already finds likely. Over a few iterations the tails get thinned out, diversity collapses, and you end up with a model that's more confident and less capable on anything slightly off-center. That's the model collapse story people talk about.

The other failure mode is when the synthetic data has structure that's correlated with something you didn't intend. Maybe the generator has a stylistic tic, or always solves problems a particular way, and the student model learns that artifact instead of the underlying skill. So the diagnostics I care about are coverage and diversity relative to the target distribution, plus some kind of verification signal, whether that's execution, a checker, or human review, so you're filtering toward correctness rather than toward whatever the generator happens to prefer. Synthetic data is really a tool for reshaping the distribution, and it's only as good as your understanding of what shape you actually need.

r001.rationale: The response describes repeated self-training on model-generated samples causing diversity collapse, but does not clearly say performance will be poor when the training data is changed to consist entirely of synthetic data.

r002.rationale: The response discusses coverage and diversity relative to a target distribution, but does not clearly state that training data should remain representative of the intended natural data distribution.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: how well does the synthetic data represent the distribution you actually care about? You can generate a lot of data, but if it mostly reflects patterns the model already knows, you may not be adding much information. And if the generator has biases or makes systematic errors, you can amplify those through training.

The tails of the distribution are particularly important. There may be rare cases that matter a lot in practice but are poorly represented in the original data. Synthetic data can help if you have a way to generate those cases and verify that they’re meaningful and correct. But simply sampling from a model doesn’t guarantee that you recover what’s missing; you may just get more examples from the most common parts of its distribution.

So I would think about coverage, quality, and the mixture with real data together. And ultimately, you need to evaluate on independent data that reflects the intended use. The number of synthetic examples alone doesn’t tell you whether they’re helping.

r001.rationale: The response warns that synthetic data can add little information or amplify errors, but it does not predict poor performance when training data consists entirely of synthetic data.

r002.rationale: It says synthetic data should represent the distribution the model is intended to learn and emphasizes coverage, quality, and evaluation on data reflecting the intended use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: how well does the synthetic data represent the distribution you actually care about? If it gives you more examples of patterns that are already well represented, you may not gain very much. But if it helps cover parts of the distribution where you have very little real data, it can be quite useful—provided those examples are accurate.

The challenge is that a model generating synthetic data has its own biases. It may produce the most likely examples and miss the rare cases. If you repeatedly train on that output, you can reinforce those biases and lose diversity. So more data doesn’t necessarily mean more information.

I would look at both the quality and the coverage of the synthetic data, and evaluate on held-out real data from the intended use case. The right mixture of real and synthetic data depends on that distribution and on what capability you’re trying to improve.

r001.rationale: The response warns that synthetic data can reinforce biases and reduce diversity, but it does not predict poor performance when training data consists entirely of synthetic data.

r002.rationale: It says synthetic data should represent the distribution of interest and that the real/synthetic mixture depends on that distribution, directly conveying that training data should reflect the intended distribution.
